title: Pick the right production read path
description: An archive-api endpoint has to serve a 'recent articles by popular authors' query under heavy load. Walk the tree to choose between read replica, cache, schema separation, or main DB.

root.question: What's the staleness tolerance of this endpoint?

options.label: Real-time required (a librarian just changed the data and the next request must see it)
Up to 60 seconds of staleness is acceptable

q-load.question: Read-after-write is required. Where should this query go?

options.label: Primary DB — the only place that has the latest committed row.

outcome.explanation: Correct. Read-after-write demands the primary. Lesson 10's read-replica config supports a read-after-write window via a 'sticky to primary for N seconds after write' policy — but the default is: real-time reads go to primary.

options.label: Read replica — async replication is usually fast enough.

outcome.explanation: Wrong. 'Usually fast enough' is the line that produces a flaky test suite and an angry user. Replication lag is bounded but real (tens to hundreds of ms typical). For real-time reads, go to primary.

options.label: Runtime cache — repopulate after each write.

outcome.explanation: Cache invalidation on writes is a separate complexity layer and still won't beat just reading from primary for a real-time-required path.

q-cache-vs-replica.question: Staleness is tolerated. Is the query expensive (joins, aggregations) or cheap?

options.label: Expensive — heavy joins, aggregations, or a big result set.

outcome.explanation: Read replica + slow-query logging. Lesson 10's setup routes reads to the replica via the driver config; the slow-query threshold log catches anything still over 100ms so you can tune indexes.

options.label: Cheap — single-row lookup hit thousands of times per second.

outcome.explanation: Replica works, but for a cheap query hit massively, an in-process LRU or a Redis cache is cheaper than a DB round-trip and avoids replication lag concerns entirely. Replica is fine — just not the best fit.

modelAnswer: Real-time-required -> primary. Tolerant of staleness + expensive query -> read replica with slow-query logging. Tolerant of staleness + cheap-but-hot query -> cache (LRU or Redis). The decision rule is staleness first, cost second. Skipping the staleness question is how a 'read replica everywhere' refactor introduces stale-read bugs in the checkout flow.

title: Production capstone quiz — explain each pick
description: Three short scenarios pulling on L1, L6, L9 and L10. Pick the right answer and explain in 15+ words for each. This is the capstone synthesis quiz.

questions.prompt: Your serverless archive-api is cold-starting in 3.1 seconds. Boot logs show 'discovering 24 entities' takes 2.4s of that. Which feature do you turn on?

options.label: GeneratedCacheAdapter (metadata cache) — write the discovered metadata to disk so the next boot loads it instead of re-discovering.
Lazy-load every entity at first use.

questions.rubric: Strong answers note the cache must be regenerated when entities change — typically as a build step — otherwise stale metadata makes the cache the bug.

questions.prompt: Production incident: report endpoint started leaking tenant B's articles to tenant A. The recent change was an admin import script using `em.disableFilter('tenant')`. What is the minimal fix?

options.label: Disable the filter only on a forked EM scoped to that one import operation, never on the global em.
Delete the tenant filter — they're too dangerous.
Throw an exception any time disableFilter is called.

questions.rubric: Reasoning should mention that em.disableFilter on the shared/global em is process-wide — all later requests reuse the same EM with the filter off. A forked EM gets its own filter state.

questions.prompt: Your Transactional Outbox processor stops draining — outbox rows pile up but no errors logged. The cron decorator is in place. What's the likely cause?

options.label: Missing @CreateRequestContext() on the cron method — the EM is shared/stale and might be in a bad state from a prior run.
Missing em.flush() at the end — processedAt is set in memory but never persisted, so the next tick re-reads the same rows... wait, that's the symptom too.
Message broker is down — but the question says no errors logged.

questions.rubric: Strong answers note that missing @CreateRequestContext() is the canonical lesson-9 bug: the cron reuses a long-lived EM, the Identity Map fills with stale references, flush eventually fails silently or rolls back.

modelAnswer: Cold start fix: metadata cache (GeneratedCacheAdapter) — but regenerate it at build, otherwise the cache becomes the bug. Tenant leak: scope the filter disable to a forked EM, never the global one. Stuck outbox processor: missing @CreateRequestContext() — the canonical lesson 9 trap where a non-HTTP entry shares the global EM and slowly poisons itself.

title: MikroORM vs Prisma at Fohlio — structured comparison with personal stakes (AI-resilient)
description:
You encountered Prisma in the NestJS course (nestjs-4-data-layer). Now compare its mental model to MikroORM's across four dimensions: (1) Unit of Work vs Prisma's per-operation approach, (2) relation loading, (3) migration tooling, (4) NestJS integration. For each dimension: state which tool wins and under what conditions, and name a concrete Fohlio service shape where that dimension would tip the decision.

AI-resilient constraint: at the end, paste your comparison into ChatGPT and ask it to summarize the winner. Then write 3 sentences explaining what the AI summary missed — specifically about your own experience with both tools across this course and the NestJS course. What nuance is invisible to an AI that has not run both tools against the same schema?

Metacognitive memo: Looking back at all 10 lessons, which homework task changed your mental model the most, and why?
modelAnswer: Rubric: A passing answer names a specific Fohlio service per dimension and avoids 'it depends' as a verdict. Unit of Work: MikroORM wins when you have multi-entity transactional flows (the outbox pattern from L9); Prisma wins for simple CRUD where the per-operation model is less to learn. Loading: MikroORM populate + Identity Map wins on read-heavy domain logic; Prisma's `include` is more discoverable for one-off queries. Migrations: Prisma's diff-against-DB is simpler day-1; MikroORM's snapshot wins on a 4-developer team where branches diverge. NestJS integration: MikroORM's RequestContext + @Transactional decorators feel more native than Prisma's client-singleton pattern. AI summary usually defaults to 'Prisma is more popular, MikroORM is more powerful' — invisible to it: the lived experience of debugging an N+1 against the same schema in both tools.
